library(lab06)

# Aim

In this lab, I worked with the knapsack problem. The goal is to choose items with the highest total value without exceeding a given weight limit. Each item can only be used once.

I wrote three functions to solve it: brute force, dynamic programming and greedy. I compared how they work and how much time they take. For the starred part, I chose section 1.1.7 and wrote a faster version of the greedy algorithm in C++ using Rcpp.

The functions take a data frame called `x`. It contains `w` for weight and `v` for value. The argument `W` is the maximum weight allowed. Each function returns a list containing the total value and the row numbers of the chosen items.

# Data

I first generated a small dataset to try the algorithms and understand their output. I used a fixed seed so I could reproduce the same values when running the report again. The weights and values are randomly generated; they are not manually entered results.

```{r my-data}
set.seed(123)
n <- 12
my_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n = n, min = 0, max = 10000)
)
head(my_objects)
```

Here `sample()` makes the item weights, and `runif()` makes the values. I used 12 items because brute force is manageable for a small input. I checked brute force and dynamic programming on the same generated objects:

```{r my-data-check}
my_brute <- brute_force_knapsack(my_objects, W = 3500)
my_dynamic <- knapsack_dynamic(my_objects, W = 3500)
my_brute
my_dynamic
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(my_brute$value, my_dynamic$value)))
```

I also used the data-generation code from the lab instructions for the examples with published expected results. That lets me compare my functions with the values shown in the assignment. The random-number generator setting matters here, because changing it would change the generated items.

```{r data}
suppressWarnings(RNGversion(min(as.character(getRversion()), "3.5.3")))
set.seed(42, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion")
n <- 2000
knapsack_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n = n, 0, 10000)
)
head(knapsack_objects)
```

# 1.1.2 Brute force search

Brute force tries every possible selection of items. An item can either be included or excluded, so there are `2^n` possible selections for `n` items. For each selection, the function checks the weight. If the weight is within the limit, it compares the value with the best one found so far.

This method finds the best possible answer, but it becomes slow as the number of items increases. In my implementation, checking each selection can take up to `n` steps, so the worst-case running time is `O(n * 2^n)`.

I tried the four examples given in the lab:

```{r brute-examples}
bf_8_3500  <- brute_force_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
bf_12_3500 <- brute_force_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 3500)
bf_8_2000  <- brute_force_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 2000)
bf_12_2000 <- brute_force_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 2000)

list(
  bf_8_3500 = bf_8_3500,
  bf_12_3500 = bf_12_3500,
  bf_8_2000 = bf_8_2000,
  bf_12_2000 = bf_12_2000
)

stopifnot(
  round(bf_8_3500$value) == 16770,
  round(bf_12_3500$value) == 16770,
  round(bf_8_2000$value) == 15428,
  round(bf_12_2000$value) == 15428
)
```

For `W = 3500`, the expected selected rows are 5 and 8. For `W = 2000`, they are 3 and 8. I compared the rounded values because the item values generated by `runif()` have decimal parts, while the lab sheet displays whole numbers.

**Time for 16 items:** The benchmark script runs brute force with the first 16 generated items and `W = 3500`. The actual time will appear in the results table after the script has been run.

# 1.1.3 Dynamic programming

Dynamic programming also finds the best possible answer. The difference is that it saves results for smaller capacities and uses them again. This avoids checking every possible subset separately.

For each item, there are two choices: leave it out, or take it if there is enough room. I keep whichever choice gives a larger total value.

For an item with weight `w_i` and value `v_i`, the calculation is:

$$
DP(i,c) = \begin{cases}
DP(i-1,c), & \text{if } w_i > c,\\
\max\{DP(i-1,c),\;v_i+DP(i-1,c-w_i)\}, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Here `c` is the current capacity and `i` is the number of items considered. The function also keeps track of which items were chosen, so it can return their original row numbers.

This method uses integer weights and an integer capacity. Its running time is `O(nW)` with a table using `O(nW)` memory. This is usually much more practical than brute force when `W` is not too large.

```{r dynamic-examples}
dp_8_3500 <- knapsack_dynamic(
  knapsack_objects[1:8, ],
  W = 3500
)

dp_12_2000 <- knapsack_dynamic(
  knapsack_objects[1:12, ],
  W = 2000
)

dp_8_3500
dp_12_2000

stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    dp_8_3500$value,
    bf_8_3500$value
  )),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    dp_12_2000$value,
    bf_12_2000$value
  ))
)
```

The values should agree with brute force, even if different optimal item combinations are possible.

**Time for 500 items:** The benchmark script uses the first 500 generated objects with `W = 3500`. The measured time will appear in the results table.

# 1.1.4 Greedy heuristic

For greedy, I first calculate `v / w`, which shows how much value an item gives for each unit of weight. I sort the items by this ratio, starting with the highest. Then I go through the sorted items and select an item if it still fits.

Greedy is much faster, but it can miss the best combination because a good individual choice does not always lead to the best final answer. My function also checks the best single item that fits and compares it with the greedy selection. Sorting takes most of the work, giving `O(n log n)` time.

```{r greedy-examples}
g_800_3500 <- greedy_knapsack(
  knapsack_objects[1:800, ],
  W = 3500
)

g_1200_2000 <- greedy_knapsack(
  knapsack_objects[1:1200, ],
  W = 2000
)

g_800_3500
g_1200_2000


# Compare my greedy results with the lab examples
cat("Greedy result for 800 items:", round(g_800_3500$value), "\n")
cat("Value shown in the lab:", 192647, "\n")

cat("Greedy result for 1200 items:", round(g_1200_2000$value), "\n")
cat("Value shown in the lab:", 212337, "\n")

# Check that the selected items are valid
check_result <- function(data, W, answer) {

  ids <- answer$elements

  stopifnot(
    all(ids %in% seq_len(nrow(data))),
    anyDuplicated(ids) == 0,
    sum(data$w[ids]) <= W,
    isTRUE(all.equal(
      sum(data$v[ids]),
      answer$value
    ))
  )
}

check_result(
  knapsack_objects[1:800, ],
  3500,
  g_800_3500
)

check_result(
  knapsack_objects[1:1200, ],
  2000,
  g_1200_2000
)

```

These are the examples printed in the lab sheet. For the 1200-item example, the capacity in the PDF is `2000`, not `3500`. The separate instructor tests also contain a 1200-item case at `W = 3500`.

**Time for one million items:** The benchmark uses the same method of generating weights and values, but with `n = 1000000`. The time is recorded by the script and shown below.

# 1.1.5 Tests

I added the original test files provided for brute force and greedy. I also wrote tests for dynamic programming by checking its results against brute force for small examples. Other tests check invalid input and compare the normal R version of greedy with the C++ version.

I use these commands in RStudio:

```{r tests, eval=FALSE}
devtools::test()
devtools::check()
```

I need all important tests and package checks to pass before submission. The original greedy test includes a very short timing limit, so I check the actual result rather than assuming it will pass on every computer.

# 1.1.6 Profiling and optimization

The `profvis` script can show which parts of the code use the most time. In the greedy function, I used a preallocated vector for selected row numbers instead of making the vector longer during each iteration. In the dynamic-programming function, I used vectorized updates for the capacity calculations.

To compare the improvements fairly, the benchmark script runs the older scalar-loop version and the optimized version with the same data. It first checks that both give the same best value. Then it measures the time taken by each version.

I calculate the performance gain as:

$$
\text{Speedup} =
\frac{\text{Time before optimization}}
{\text{Time after optimization}}.
$$

The measured values appear in the table below after running the scripts. I also need to describe the actual `profvis` output in my own words before submitting.

# 1.1.7 First starred task: Rcpp

I chose the first starred task. I added an argument `fast` to `greedy_knapsack()`. Its default is `FALSE`, so the function still works when `fast` is not supplied. When `fast = TRUE`, the selection part runs in C++ through Rcpp.

I kept the same greedy sorting and item-selection rules in R and C++, so the answers can be compared directly. Since C++ counts array positions from 0 but R counts from 1, the C++ version converts the chosen positions before returning them to R.

```{r rcpp-demo}
r_answer <- greedy_knapsack(
  knapsack_objects[1:800, ],
  3500,
  fast = FALSE
)

cpp_answer <- greedy_knapsack(
  knapsack_objects[1:800, ],
  3500,
  fast = TRUE
)

r_answer
cpp_answer

stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(r_answer, cpp_answer))
)
```

To answer the Rcpp speed question, I run both versions with exactly the same one-million-item data. The speedup is the R time divided by the C++ time.

# Performance results

I run the following from the package project folder before building the vignette:

```{r benchmark-instructions, eval=FALSE}
devtools::install()

source("inst/scripts/benchmark_lab6.R")
source("inst/scripts/profile_lab6.R")
source("inst/scripts/benchmark_optimization.R")

devtools::build_vignettes()
```

The tables below show the measurements saved by the scripts. 

```{r tables, results='asis'}
locate_results <- function(filename) {

  candidates <- c(
    file.path("..", "inst", "extdata", filename),
    file.path("inst", "extdata", filename),
    system.file(
      "extdata",
      filename,
      package = "lab06"
    )
  )

  found <- candidates[
    nzchar(candidates) &
    file.exists(candidates)
  ]

  if (length(found)) {
    found[1]
  } else {
    ""
  }
}

bench_file <- locate_results(
  "benchmark_results.csv"
)

optimization_file <- locate_results(
  "optimization_results.csv"
)

if (nzchar(bench_file)) {

  benchmark <- read.csv(bench_file)

  print(knitr::kable(
    benchmark,
    caption = "Measured lab timings",
    digits = 4
  ))

  if (
    nrow(benchmark) == 4L &&
    all(is.finite(benchmark$elapsed_seconds)) &&
    benchmark$elapsed_seconds[4] > 0
  ) {

    cat(sprintf(
      "\n**Measured Rcpp speedup:** %.3f times.\n\n",
      benchmark$elapsed_seconds[3] /
        benchmark$elapsed_seconds[4]
    ))
  }

} else {

  cat(
    "**PENDING: run the main benchmark in RStudio and rebuild the vignette.**\n\n"
  )
}

if (nzchar(optimization_file)) {

  optimization <- read.csv(
    optimization_file
  )

  print(knitr::kable(
    optimization,
    caption = "Measured dynamic-programming optimization",
    digits = 4
  ))

  if (
    nrow(optimization) == 2L &&
    all(is.finite(optimization$elapsed_seconds)) &&
    optimization$elapsed_seconds[2] > 0
  ) {

    cat(sprintf(
      "\n**Measured optimization gain:** %.3f times.\n\n",
      optimization$elapsed_seconds[1] /
        optimization$elapsed_seconds[2]
    ))
  }

} else {

  cat(
    "**PENDING: run the optimization benchmark and rebuild the vignette.**\n\n"
  )
}
```
